Direct measurement of hydrogen diffusion coefficients in materials is not a difficult task, yet, to understand mechanisms behind the diffusion and to design materials resistant to hydrogen embrittlement should be relatively harder, because the breakdown of this comprehension task often involves too small-scale problems beyond reach of experiments [4].

Take a typical iron-based material, which is composed of grains, grain boundaries, and defects, as an example, diffusion of hydrogen in the material should be understood by analyzing behaviors of hydrogen in these regions separately, if following the concepts from the reductionism.
This limitation can be complemented by computer simulations.
Numerical studies based on molecular dynamics become helpful when encountering too small-scale problems in materials research.
The molecular dynamics method has found applications in many materials like polymers [9], cement [10], biomaterials [11], hydrogel [12], carbon nanotubes [13], metal [14], etc.
On hydrogen diffusion in metals, the method has been widely validated and used.
The GBs of iron are found traps of hydrogen, especially in triple junctions, and the grain size of iron would decide hydrogen diffusion properties [1517].

Aggregation of hydrogen would suppress the dislocation emission at the crack tip and lead to a ductile-to-brittle transition [23], and subsequent molecular dynamics studies involve more versatile structures [24,25], alloys [26, 27], and more realistic configurations [28].

The computation includes a high-throughput molecular dynamics method as an engine to generate data, and a deep neural network that reads in structural data and yields diffusion coefficient of hydrogen as an end-to-end algorithm.

Diffusion coefficients of hydrogen is obtained via calculating the mean squared displacement (MSD) of hydrogen atom in iron with varied configurations, of which the key parameters are rotations of upper and bottom iron grain, represented in axis-angle form.
The diffusion coefficient is computed using Eq. (1).
The force field is EAM, with parameters from an existing study [30].
Other technical parameters include (i) timestep at 1fs, (ii) LAMMPS [31] for simulation and OVITO [32] for visualization, (iii) MSD collected every 100 steps, (iv) box size about 2.8 nm.
The diffusion of hydrogen in the entire piece of material can be evaluated by global consideration of all local regions.
The simulation box is divided into an upper and a bottom region, with different orientations.
We employ a Monte-Carlo method to draw samples (rotations) from the SO(3) group, and each rotation is represented in axis-angle form.

To ensure an even distribution over a sphere, the rotation axis is drawn from the angular coordinates, i.e., theta (azimuthal angle) and phi (polar angle) instead of generating three random numbers for the axis components.
The axis vector can then be derived from these angles using spherical coordinates.
The rotation angle is randomized from 0 to 360 degrees.
Schematically, the distribution of the generated rotations is plotted in Fig. 2.
The constructed model is then sent to annealing and subsequent diffusion simulations.
The symmetry of the body centered cubic (bcc) crystal is not considered in this sampling step.
Instead, the data collected can be augmented according to the symmetry of bcc structure, thus adding bias (physical knowledge) gained from the symmetry of iron crystal to the machine learning model.
The SchNet [35,36] architecture is employed in this study, with modifications on the embedding layer.
To activate the embedding layer, we first run a polyhedral template matching (PTM) [37] algorithm on the annealed atomistic structure, and then bin the root-mean-square deviation (RMsD) into 100
Consequently, iron atoms can be classified into 100 types, which are then sent to the embedding layer to obtain a 64-dimension vector for subsequent data forwarding.
Details of the SchNet can be found in Fig. 3 as well as existing studies.

The training process of the network is intuitive, with the input being atomistic data of each model (can be regarded as a collection of scattered points in 3-d space) and the output being a scalar value, natural log of the diffusion coefficient of hydrogen in this model.
A comparison between the numerical and experimental [38] results is shown in Fig. 4.

We find that the employed EAM force field parameters yield accepted results at about 1000 K and 300 K, whereas in the range around 500 K, the calculated diffusion coefficients are usually lower than experiments and show some divergences between each run.

Despite the deficiency, we show that the employed EAM parameters can yield (i) predictions of hydrogen diffusion in iron with accepted accuracy at 333 K and (ii) the deviations between parallel runs are not huge.
The present molecular dynamics simulations all show that the structural deviations from BCC iron leads to decrease in hydrogen diffusion.
The diffusion coefficients above $1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ cm²/s are not shown.
In iron, atoms with non-BCC structure could exist near dislocations or grain boundaries, both of which can slow diffusion of hydrogen.
It turns out that the diffusion of hydrogen of a system can be evaluated by looping over its subsystems and averaging.

This observation critically justifies the deep neural network, because the dataflow in the network is all atomwise, until a summation pooling is attached to the end, to yield the diffusion coefficient of hydrogen.
The modified SchNet behaves accurately in predicting hydrogen diffusion coefficient of a variety of GB structure of α-iron.
Plots of training and validation loss in log scale are shown in Fig. 6.

During the training, we also see fluctuations in the training loss around 0.06, accompanied by a similar trend in the validation loss, suggesting that the employed network may have undergone escapes from a local minimal and avoided over fitting.
The reason for this rare error could be the existence of a rare local configuration of atoms in that model, which is unseen in the training set.
Furthermore, this inaccuracy can also be handled by more abundant sampling if the computational framework is put to practical applications.

Intuitively, this evaluation can be performed repeatedly over the entire domain of a material, and all the local diffusion coefficients can be combined into a grid analysis to obtain the global diffusion coefficients of the materials, as described in Fig. 7.

The fundamental concept involves initially decomposing the complex material into small, localized regions with random atomistic structures (sampled from a rational distribution of material compositions), subsequently employing molecular dynamics simulations or machine learning-based approaches to estimate local material properties, and ultimately aggregating the local information to evaluate the overall material performance.
However, it is important to note that this bottom-up approach is still in its nascent stages.

To achieve a comprehensive multi-scale scheme, further developments are necessary, including (i) the advancement of high-throughput or large-scale molecular dynamics methods to incorporate a wider range of elements (for alloys and oxides) and more variations in atomistic structures (such as dislocations and grain boundaries), and (ii) the progression of smallscale measurement techniques to provide more detailed knowledge about the material's atomistic structure, enabling more accurate sampling of atomistic models.

Within this multi-scale computational framework, the trained neural network serves as a surrogate model that performs two key functions: first, it evaluates physical properties (such as hydrogen atom diffusion coefficients) based on local atomic configurations, and second, it updates parameters for higher-scale numerical methods.
This could further create an iterative feedback loop, with atomic positions' update in the numerical simulation and material properties' update by the surrogate model.
Such iterative coupling enables large-scale simulations that retain atomic-level precision while maintaining computational efficiency.
This approach bridges the gap between atomistic detail and macroscopic behavior, allowing for more comprehensive materials modeling.
The trained network can be embedded in a multiscale scheme to analyze polycrystalline structure in grids and to include more numerical methods across the length scales, forming a bottom-up approach.

Over the past decade, there have been and currently are still ongoing significant research and industrial strives to develop and manufacture advanced metallic materials via additive manufacturing, which hold great promise for structural, functional, and engineering applications [14].

Additive manufacturing, as a bottomup technique, has obvious advantages over traditional subtractive methods in manufacturing complex-shaped structural parts, not to mention its efficient material usage [1].

As of now, additive manufacturing has made great progress in the fabrication of traditional single-component alloy systems, such as Fe-based stainless steel (SS) [2,5], Ni-based alloys [6], Ti alloys [3,7], Al alloys [8], Mg alloys [9], and Cu alloys [10] regarding good comprehensive properties (mechanical and corrosion properties).

In particular, taking the additively manufactured 316 L SS as an example, it not only possesses superior mechanical properties to its conventional wrought counterpart, but its corrosion resistance, especially pitting resistance, is also significantly improved, which is attributed to the unique microstructure and the reduction of MnS inclusions caused by the thermal distortions and rapid cooling during the additive manufacturing process [1113].

The emerging HEAs with widely tunable compositions represent a new alloy design concept, which breaks through the conventional alloy design strategies based on the single-principle element and expands the alloy design repertoire for more possible alloying element combinations [15].

In recent years, some representative HEAs via additive manufacturing have been successfully prepared and exhibited satisfactory comprehensive mechanical properties, such as Cantor alloy [16,17], $\mathrm { F e } _ { 5 0 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 3 0 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 1 0 } \mathrm { C r } _ { 1 0 }$ dual-phase alloy [18], equiatomic FeNiCr alloy [19], L12-strengthed $( \mathsf { C o C r N i } ) _ { 9 4 } \mathsf { A l } _ { 3 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 3 }$ alloy [20], L12-strengthed $( \mathrm { F e C o N i } ) _ { 8 6 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 7 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 7 }$ alloy [21], AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA [22], refractory HEAs [23], etc.

Admittedly, the compositional inhomogeneities due to the $\mathrm { L } 1 _ { 2 }$ precipitation coupled with the intrinsic elemental segregation (usually at the cellular boundaries) of the additively manufactured microstructures poses a significant challenge to the corrosion resistance of L12-strengthened HEAs fabricated by additive manufacturing.
In this study, a novel additively manufactured Al5Ti5 HEA was first successfully prepared using the SLM technique.

We expect that the present work represents future research direction towards corrosion-resistant additively manufactured HEAs and will inspire waves of efforts to develop high-performance L12-strengthened HEAs for advanced structural applications in aggressive environments.

The SLM was performed using a laser powder-bed-fusion (L-PBF) printer (SLM-100, Guangdong Hanbang) under an argon atmosphere with optimized printing parameters (laser power: 175 W, scan speed: 1000 mm/s, layer thickness: 30 µm, hatching space: 80 μm).

To be more precise, the Marangoni force, which is the tangential component of surface tension, is generated by the surface gradient of the temperature field, and the magnitude of the Marangoni force depends on the temperature distribution at the surface.
Thus, strong Marangoni flows will develop on the molten pool surface, which causes the liquid metal to flow from the center region to the boundary of the molten pool [57].

In particular, the motion of interfaces is the dominant mechanism in grain growth (2, 3), recrystallization (4, 5), first-order phase transformations (6, 7), plastic deformation of nanocrystalline materials (8, 9), and polarization switching in ferroic materials (10, 11).

There has been extensive literature over the past several decades that suggests that diverse oscillatory fields (thermal, mechanical, electrical, magnetic, etc.) can enhance the grain growth rate by up to 1500% and the recrystallization rate by up to 300%; these findings are summarized in table S6.

However, the mechanism by which the activation energy reduction arises from the oscillation in the fields remains unclear.
We show that the Brownian ratchet model provides an explanation for this mechanism.

Given the observed directional dependency of GB mobility, it is important to revise the classical kinetic equation for GB motion—i.e., $v = M F ,$ where v is the GB velocity, F is the driving force, and M is the GB mobility.

Once we reverse the direction of the driving force— i.e., F → F−the classical equation predicts that the GB velocity becomes -v, which is inconsistent with our analysis, MD simulations, and several experimental observations.
This issue can be resolved by modifying the mobility to make it a function of the sign of F—i.e., M(F/|F|).

In addition, the velocity of nonsymmetric GBs should, as a general rule, be nonzero when the driving force F is oscillatory (even when the mean force $\bar { F } = 0 )$ and/or the temperature Tis cycled.

The equation for GB motion may be empirically rewritten in the form $v = M \bar { F } + \mathsf { a } ( \Omega \Delta F / k _ { \mathrm { B } } \bar { T } ) +$ $\beta e ^ { - \gamma / f _ { T } } ( \Delta T / \hat { T } )$ , where M is a function of the sign of the mean driving force $\bar { F } / | \bar { F } |$ and the mean temperature T; ΔF and ΔT are the amplitudes of the driving force and temperature oscillations; $f _ { T }$ is the cyclic annealing frequency; Ω is the atomic volume; $k _ { \mathrm { B } }$ is the Boltzmann constant; and α, β, and γ are parameters that are functions of temperature, material, and GB structure.
Such a modified equation for GB motion incorporates steady and oscillatory driving forces and cyclic annealing effects.

This expression may be used in any phenomenological model for microstructure evolution with assumed (or measured) values of the parameters, allowing for more realistic descriptions of GB motion as well as a guide for designing thermomechanical processing to manipulate microstructures.

The implication of direction-dependent GB mobility and the effects of oscillatory fields are potentially important for interpreting experimental observations of GB motion in a polycrystal and for simulating microstructure evolution.

Specifically, microstructure evolution simulations should not assume that the mobility of a GB is constant [a conclusion reached by others but for other reasons (38)] nor that mobilities can be correctly extracted from experiments by monitoring averaged mobilities.

For example, the direction of GB motion during microstructure evolution may switch as a result of the topological change in microstructure, and the direction-averaged mobility has no physical meaning.

Traditional structural materials, often composed of a single phase, frequently struggle to meet the evolving demands of high-performance and lightweight applications in industries such as aerospace [1, 2], bioengineering [3, 4], automotive [5], and other fields [6, 7].
As a result, the integration of compositional and functional gradation in materials has become a key focus in modern manufacturing [8, 9].
To address these challenges, dual-phase materials have been extensively investigated.
This transformation facilitates deformation twins formation, ultimately leading to the phase interface converting into a perfect twin boundary, enhancing mechanical performance [10].

However, due to limited fabricating control over composition and spatial structure, conventional fabrication techniques such as casting or forging struggle to produce phase-tunable materials with tailored microstructures.

Additive manufacturing (AM) has become a transformative method for developing high-performance alloys, including magnesium alloys [11], NiTi shape memory alloy [1216], copper matrix composites [17], aluminum matrix composites [18], and titanium alloys [1921].
While various powder-spreading systems have been developed, their high costs and low efficiency in fabricating tailored chemical powders remain significant challenges [2426].

This is attributed to the effect of rule-of-mixture and hetero-deformation strengthening, which redistribute stress away from the soft to hard regions, ultimately improving global yield strength [28].

The embrittlement of a material that has hydrogen dissolved within the matrix prior to loading has been termed internal hydrogen embrittlement (IHE) while the embrittlement of a material in a hydrogen environment has been described as hydrogen environment embrittlement (HEE).
Materials have been shown to behave differently HEE and IHE conditions [5,811].

It has been proposed that for most engineering materials, the embrittlement due to hydrogen, whether HEE or IHE, is not from the uniformly distributed hydrogen in the matrix, but the hydrogen segregated to microstructural inhomogeneities [1,12].

It was suggested that the difference between IHE and HEE may be related to a change in the characteristic fracture distance with no change in embrittlement mechanism [8], a change in both the characteristic distance and the embrittlement mechanism [5], or no change in either embrittlement mechanism or characteristic distance [11].
A well characterized material is required to compare the IHE and HEE behavior.
The material used for this comparison is alloy X-750.
The HEE studies for this alloy have all previously been performed in an aqueous environment where the hydrogen fugacity is not well characterized [7,14,15].
An evaluation of all the data is provided and a model to describe the behavior is developed based on an understanding of the materialenvironment interaction.
This work shows, similar to the work by Gerberich on steels [8], that the characteristic fracture distance is dierent for IHE and HEE.
Walter, Jewett, and coworkers have published numerous papers on the role of hydrogen on the behavior of structural materials using uniaxial tensile and notched tensile specimens [5,10].
It was further shown for the uniaxial type specimen that some alloys, for example alloy 718 or Rene' 41, are extremely susceptible to HEE but the embrittlement due to IHE was negligible.
Fritzmeier, Walter, Meisels, and Jewett also investigated alloy 903, a FCC FeNi-base precipitation strengthened superalloy [10].
In their analysis, it was shown that the same modeling approach satisfactorily described the fracture behavior for both IHE and HEE of steels.
In this work, like the work of Moody and coworkers, the model was based on achieving a critical hydrogen concentration at a characteristic distance ahead of the crack tip.
It was shown that for HEE the characteristic distance is much nearer to the crack tip than for IHE while the mechanism did not appear to change.

Two aspects have mainly motivated these endeavours.
Significant progress has been achieved in the development of computational models for hydrogen-assisted fracture.

Multi-physics phase field fracture models have been particularly successful, demonstrating their ability to capture complex cracking conditions, such as nucleation from multiple sites or the coalescence of numerous defects, in arbitrary geometries and dimensions [22,23].
However, the surge in modelling efforts experienced in the context of monotonic, static fracture has not been observed in fatigue.
Moreover, the success of phase field formulations in predicting hydrogen-assisted static fracture has not been extended to fatigue yet.

The main elements of the coupled deformationdiffusion-fatigue formulation presented are: (i) a thermodynamicallyconsistent extension of Fick's law of mass diffusion, (ii) a fatigue history variable and associated degradation function, (iii) a phase field description of crack-solid interface evolution, (iv) a penaltybased formulation to update environmental boundary conditions, and (v) an atomistically-inspired relation between the hydrogen content and the fracture surface energy.

This novel variational framework is numerically implemented in the context of the finite element method and used to model hydrogen-assisted fatigue in several boundary value problems of particular interest.
We show how the model captures the main experimental trends; namely, the sensitivity of fatigue crack growth rates to the loading frequency and the environment.
Finally, Virtual SN curves are computed for both smooth and notched samples, exhibiting a promising agreement with experimental data.

•The crack tip hydrogen distribution is very sensitive to the loading frequency f and the material diffusivity D.
• The model adequately captures the sensitivity of fatigue crack growth rates to hydrogen content.
• The model naturally recovers the Paris law behaviour and thus can quantify the influence of hydrogen on the Paris law parameters.
• Virtual S-N curves are obtained for various environments and both notched and smooth samples.

Additive manufacturing (AM) represents manufacturing processes that fabricate parts through the addition of material in a layer-by-layer fashion.

Advantages when using AM technologies can include such things as time and cost reduction, minimal human interaction, less waste creation, and reduced geometric shape constraints (Wong and Hernandez, 2012).
Along with PBF, binder jetting is an emerging lower cost technology for the fabrication of metallic components.
For example, binder jetting offers a versatile range of materials for fabrication, and is currently being utilized for sand mold and casting applications (Wohlers, 2017).
PBF processes, however, are already being employed in the biomedical and aerospace markets.

For example, \~50,000 hip implants fabricated using electron beam melting (EBM, a tradename for EPBF) have been implanted in patients today, while General Electric has undergone manufacture of its LEAP engine fuel nozzles using direct metal laser melting (DMLM, a tradename for LPBF) providing them with higher life cycles while reducing overall weight and production costs (Wohlers, 2017).
Nickel-based superalloys such as Inconel 718 and 625 have seen widespread adoption in multiple fields due to the alloys' multipurpose capabilities and range of applications.

While conventional manufacturing of components using these high-performance alloys has been difficult due to excessive tool wear and low material removal rates, the use of powder-based AM technologies can remove these constraints while also improving lead times and reducing manufacturing costs (Costes et al., 2007; Buchbinder et al., 2011).

Inconel 625 can best be described as a nickel-based superalloy that exhibits excellent mechanical strength, resistance to thermal deformation, good surface stability and resistance to oxidation (Rai et al., 2004).

text: Inconel 625 consists mostly of nickel (61.0 wt%) and chromium (21.5 wt%) with other alloying elements including molybdenum, niobium, and iron (Eiselstein and Tillack, 1991).

For PBF AM, the chemical requirements (in wt%) for Inconel 625 include: Cr at 20-23%, Mo at 8- 10%, Niobium at 3.15-4.15%, and maximum wt% for C at 0.10, Mn at 0.50, Si at 0.50, P at 0.015, S at 0.015, Co at 1.00, Ti at 0.40, Al at 0.40 and Fe at 5.00, with the remainder of Ni (ASTM International, 2014a).
Inconel alloys are known as superalloys because of their excellent mechanical strength and resistance to creep and corrosion in harsh environments.

Inconel 625 has found widespread and diverse applications in the aerospace, marine service and petrochemical industries due to the excellent combination of strength, resulting from age hardening, at both ambient and elevated temperatures, as well as corrosion resistance (Rai et al., 2004).

In the aerospace industry, gas turbine engine exhaust systems, spray bars, thrust reverser systems, turbine shroud rings, fuel/ hydraulic line tubing and bellows, are just a few examples of components where Inconel 625 is used (Floreen et al., 1994).

Inconel 625 components have been manufactured using several conventional manufacturing processes such as casting, powder metallurgy, spray forming, weld overlaying and co-extrusion of piping components (Song and Nakata, 2010).
As the demand and growth of AM continues, fabrication using AM with Inconel 625 has emerged as a promising method for part production.

Therefore, the focus of this research is a characterization of Inconel 625 components fabricated by three different powder-bedbased AM technologies with an emphasis on comparing the mechanical properties of components manufactured with each technology.
Each technology has associated benefits, and efforts are ongoing to compete with conventional production processes across several industries, despite each technology's unique differences.
The three AM technologies evaluated in this study consist of two PBF processes, including EPBF and LPBF, and the binder jetting process.
Results were then compared to ASTM standards established for AM fabrication of Inconel 625.

Binder Jetting is defined as an "additive manufacturing process in which a liquid bonding agent is selectively deposited to join powder materials," according to ISO/ASTM 52900 (ASTM International, 2015).
It is an AM process in which parts are fabricated in a layer-by-layer fashion using a polymer-based or aqueous binder.
This process is repeated until the part is complete.

Parts fabricated via binder jetting must undergo two essential post-fabrication processes: (1) binder curing (referred to as drying by ExOne, the manufacturer of the system studied herein) and (2) sintering.
As per ISO/ASTM 52900, powder bed fusion is defined as "an additive manufacturing process in which thermal energy selectively fuses regions of a powder bed" (ASTM International, 2015).
The fabrication of metal components is achieved by controlling the powder fusion to a prescribed region at the given layer as commanded by a CAD design, followed by the creation of a new layer.
The EPBF process is an AM technique used for fabrication of metallic components through the use of an electron beam as the energy source to melt powder particles together.
The process can be broken down into three major steps: (1) raking of a powder layer, (2) preheating of powder particles (sintering), and (3) melting of the powder particles.

EPBF can process a vast variety of materials and Arcam, the manufacturer of the EPBF equipment used here, has commercially released parameters for materials such as the titanium alloy Ti6Al4V, Ti6Al4V ELI, titanium grade 2, Arcam ASTM F75 cobaltchrome, and nickel-based superalloy Inconel 718 (Arcam, 2011).
The LPBF process accomplishes the fusion of powder particles with the use of a laser beam as the thermal energy source.
The LPBF fabrication process is completed in an inert gas environment (argon or nitrogen), differing from EPBF.
A blade mechanism spreads a new powder layer onto the build area, where the laser beam then selectively fuses powder particles together, generating fully dense components (Bremen et al., 2012).
LPBF technology has achieved success in the fabrication of titanium alloys, stainless steel, tool steels, aluminum, cobalt chrome and nickel based alloys (SLM Solutions, 2018).
Binder jetting specimens were fabricated by the ExOne Company using an M-Flex system (ExOne, North Huntingdon, PA, USA) with an ethylene glycol monobutyl ether (aqueous-based) binder.
Both PBF fabricated specimens were built at the W.M.

The mechanical testing results indicated that all three technologies were able to surpass the minimum values for UTS, % elongation, and YS that are required by the ASTM standard F3056-14, achieving equivalent properties to wrought Inconel 625 for the X build orientation specimens.
LPBF fabricated samples performed with the most uniformity in the majority of the mechanical properties evaluated, with both orientations satisfying the minimum ASTM standard requirements.
The uniqueness of each technology brings a degree of variability that affects the properties of a printed part.
Therefore, it is important to determine which technology is most adequate and best suited for a particular application.

Nevertheless, with the ability for the three technologies to exceed the minimum standard requirements, it can be stated that these techniques can be used effectively for fabrication of Inconel 625 components, at least in the X build orientation.
One such example is the fatigue performance for components fabricated using each AM technique, which might be the subject of further research.

The strain partitioning has two origins at two different scales.
One is macroscopic across the whole sample thickness, while the other is microscopic between the domain interior and walls of each parallelepiped domain.

Both types of strain partitioning evolve during tensile testing due to the dependence of the γ → α′ -martensite transformation with applied tensile strains and the austenite stability of domain sizes as well.
In this sense, the dynamic strain partitioning is expected, similar to that in TRIP-maraging steel [12].

Furthermore, the whole gradient structured sample can be approximately regarded as the integration of many thin layers with increasing Hv toward the surface [34].
The plastic deformation occurs in sequence of neighboring layers with low to high flow stresses.
The strain partitioning at the macroscale is, actually, an intrinsic property of the gradient structure due to the presence of the initial Hv gradient.

In addition, this Hv difference will be increased after the onset of the $\gamma \ \to \ \alpha ^ { \prime }$ -martensite trans formation in the domain walls upon further straining as seen in Fig. 10(a) and (b).

In other words, dynamic strain partitioning occurs microscopically in each parallelepiped domain and continues until the final stage of uniform deformation.
The dynamic strain partitioning is associated with the mechanical incompatibility at both the macroscale and microscale.
Firstly, two interfaces exist, demarcating the elastic and plastic layers in the gradient structure during tensile deformation.
Mechanical incompatibility is produced at elastic/plastic interfaces.
As a result, dynamic strain partitioning causes an enhanced uniform ductility, especially when strain partitioning lasts up to the end of uniform deformation.

This will lead to tensile lateral stress in the CG layer and compressive lateral stress in the gradient layers.

Since the $\gamma  a$ transformation is accompanied with volume expansion, the lateral tensile stress should promote the phase transformation [60,61], which is the reason why the onset of the $\gamma \to \pmb { \mathscr { a } } ^ { \prime }$ martensitic transformation for the CG layer is shifted to lower tensile strains in gradient structured samples.
Interestingly, a strong delay of the $\gamma \to \mathfrak { a }$ transformation is visible in the gradient layers as seen in Fig. 9(b).
Second, the gradient layer only bears a lower plastic strain than the CG core due to the strain partitioning.

It is further deduced from Figs. 1 and 9(b) that the $\gamma \to \pmb { \mathscr { a } } ^ { \prime }$ martensite transformation is controlled not only by the strain level and local stress state as discussed above, but also by the applied stress level.
There exists probably a minimum stress level to trigger the phase transformation.

The free-standing $\mathsf { G L } _ { 5 } ^ { 0 . 0 4 }$ film starts the plastic deformation at very high stresses, which is why the $\gamma \to \pmb { \mathscr { a } } ^ { \prime }$ -martensitic transformation may start almost immediately upon plastic deformation.
In the gradient structure the α' -martensite transformation takes place in the whole strain range from 0.1 to the sample failure, as seen in Fig. 9(b).

In other words, the gradient structure enables the α′ -martensite transformation, and consequently the TRIP effect, to last over a large strain rage, which effectively increases the uniform elongation.
Taking the ${ \sf G S } _ { 5 } ^ { 1 }$ sample as an example, the α' martensite transformation is prolonged to the strain of more than 0.3, as compared to \~0.25 in the CG sample (see Fig. 9(b)).
The combination of the gradient structure and the TRIP effect produces a combination of strength and ductility that is superior to what was reported earlier, as shown in Fig. 11.
The gradient layers consist of parallelepiped austenite domains separated by hard ε martensite walls, and a domain size gradient along the depth.

During tensile testing of the gradient structured 304ss samples, the CG core starts plastic deformation first, while the gradient layer is still deforming elastically, causing macroscopic strain partitioning and mechanical incompatibility, which consequently produces a tensile lateral stress in the CG core and compressive lateral stress in the gradient layers.
In addition, smaller domain size in the gradient layer also delays the α' -martensite transformation.
In other words, the gradient structure can spread the TRIP effect over a larger strain range to enhance ductility.

The multiple plastic responses, including the dynamic strain partitioning and phase transformation intrinsically inter-linked with each other and cocontribute to the observed superior mechanical properties.

Recently, heterostructur materials (HMs) have been report to exbit superior tensil propertis that urpass those of theihomogeneous counterparts.Classical HMs with heterogeneity in the length scale less than a few hundred nanometres attribute their enhanced mechanical performance mainly to the hetero-deformation induced (HDI) hardening.

So far, a majority of reported HMs are fabricated by a series of conventional manufacturing methods, such as rolling plus annealing [7], powder metallurgy plus rolling [8], ball milling plus sintering [9], etc.

For instance, heterostructured titanium alloys made by L-DED exhibit a synergistic improvement in their strength and ductility [22]; A spatially heterostructured steel exhibits an over 21 % higher yield strength than the constitutional materials by switching between two powder feedstocks [24]; A radial HS offers over 33 % increases in strength compared with its monolithic counterparts [25].

Previous studies on the deformation mechanisms in HMs mainly focus on the effect of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) hardening [21, 22,24,26,27], emphasising the pile-up of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) at the interfaces between the hard and soft phases.
However, L-DED fabricated HMs typically have lamella widths on the mesoscale, i.e., \~100 µm  10 mm [24,27,34], leaving it questionable for the HDI hardening to be dominant.
While these are critical aspects in strengthening HMs, they are limited to specific structures and/or material compositions.

Specifically, the questions we aim to answer are: (i) What are the tensile strength and ductility that we can achieve in bi-metallic HSs made by L-DED? (ii) What is the dominating mechanism that leads to the improvements in the tensile strength and ductility of bi-metallic HSs? (ii) How can one design the bi-metallic HS parameters, including the lamella thickness, the material volume friction, and the number of interfaces, to achieve HSs with improved tensile strength and ductility?
The materials used in this work for sample fabrication are the 316L and PH174 stainless steels.
All samples were fabricated using an in-house developed 3-axis L-DED system equipped with an 1 kW fibre laser (IPG Photonics Corporation).
During the fabrication process, the powders were delivered by argon as the carrier and purge gas through a coaxial printing nozzle (COAX14 v5, Fraunhofer USA, Inc.).

Both the hatch spacing (hs) and the number of passes $( n _ { \mathrm { p } } )$ before powder switching were changed to achieve varying lamellae width.

Most structural metals and alloys strained in tension fail by necking that sets in when a maximum on the engineering stress—strain curve is reached.
An excellent survey focussing on various aspects of the complexity of strain localization during plastic deformation of metals has been provided recently by Antolovich and Armstrong [1].

Controlling influences of temperature, strain rate, grain size and deformation mode on strain localization are evaluated and the critical role of dislocation mechanisms in strain localization is highlighted.
The ductility issue is particularly acute for high strength materials, which usually possess a limited capability to deform uniformly.
The analysis of a large body of experimental data accumulated in numerous experimental studies [4] suggests that strength and ductility are mutually exclusive.
Substantial efforts have therefore been invested in developing conceptual frameworks and methodologies for ductility enhancement [3,5—8].

The most common explanation for the limited ductility of UFG materials is given in terms of the Considère instability criterion [9], which signifies the onset of necking at the point where the strain hardening coefficient h drops below the value of the flow stress ofor a given plastic strain rate e.
This criterion is purely mechanistic [1,10], as it is based solely on the true stress vs. true strain relation.

Although the ductility of a material is almost inevitably sacrificed after moderate pre-strain, e.g. after the very first ECAP pass, an appreciable improvement of ductility is often observed for giant pre-strains (e.g. with for the number of ECAP passes as large as 1625) [12,17].
However, it appears to be reasonably homogeneous at a macroscopic scale until necking sets in, the cross-sectional area of the specimen shrinks, and the load-displacement curve begins to drop off.

Virtually all instability criteria, including the Considère one, Eq. (1), are based entirely on the constitutive relation between stress and strain, despite the fact that strain cannot be regarded as a state variable.

Additive Manufacturing (AM) of complex components based on nickel-based superalloys is increasingly adopted in the aerospace and energy sector [1,2].
Examples of such applications include turbine blades, compressor blades and blisks, gas burners, and fuel injectors [38].
The MAR-M247 superalloy was initially developed for vacuum investment casting of turbine components by the Martin Marietta Corporation in the early 1970s [10].
After casting, the alloy requires a solution-treatment and age-hardening, typically in multiple steps [11].
Due to the obtainable high volume fraction of γ'-phase, the alloy is prone to lose its ductility through precipitation hardening that occurs within the range of aging temperatures of the alloy.
Binder Jetting (BJ), as a promising alternative metal AM process, has the potential to overcome these limitations by its process-inherent separation between the form-shaping and fusing step.

Consequently, Binder Jetting does not only possess the ability to process a wide range of materials, including non-weldable materials but also pushes the level of achievable productivity within metal AM.
Hot-isostatic-pressing (HIP) is considered to be a promising post-processing treatment in other metal AM processes such as LPBF and EBM to remove the remaining porosity [26].

Since the emergence of the equiatomic FeMnCoCrNi HEA with the face-centered cubic (fcc) structure (i.e., the famous Cantor alloy), HEAs with body-centered cubic (bcc), hexagonal close-packed (hcp) and dual-phase (fcc + bcc/fcc + hcp) structures have been developed successively [15].
They are expected to be applied in industrial fields such as aerospace, polar ships and the storage/transportation of new energy resources [69].
The mechanical properties of metallic materials are significantly influenced by plastic deformation mechanisms. [1012].
To improve the overall mechanical properties of these alloys, researchers have made numerous efforts [1319].
For instance, twinninginduced plasticity (TWIP) and/or transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effects have been introduced by reducing the stacking fault energy (SFE) of fcc HEAs.
They discovered strain localization within the FeCoCrNiPd HEA, leading to compositional fluctuations at the atomic level.
This induced significant dislocation cross-slip during plastic deformation, thereby enhancing the strength of alloy.
For instance, the creation of gradient structures allows fcc HEAs to achieve a superior combination of strength and ductility, thereby addressing the strength-ductility tradeoff [3740].
A gradient structure features microstructural characteristics—such as grain size, twin thickness and lamellar thickness—that gradually change from the surface to the center of the material.

During plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) can be generated at the interfaces of these gradient structures due to the differing mechanical properties in various regions, leading to additional strengthening and hardening of the materials [4146].

For example, Pan et al. [38] developed a multi-scaled gradient dislocation cell structure in the fcc $\mathrm { { A l } _ { 0 . 1 } \mathrm { { C o C r F e N i } } }$ HEA through cyclic torsion (CT), improving the yield strength from 150 MPa in the base alloy to 520 MPa while maintaining a uniform elongation of 45 %.

Metallic materials often require surface treatment in practical engineering applications to enhance machining surface quality, including surface hardness, roughness and wear resistance $[ 4 7 , 4 8 ]$ .
Grinding is one of the most common surface treatment methods, utilizing cutting tools to remove excess layers from the workpiece's surface, thereby meeting surface quality requirements [49,50].

It employs laser preheating, which reduces the surface hardness and brittleness, leading to a decrease in the grinding force generated during processing and ultimately improving the machining surface quality [5153].
Notably, during LAG, the machined workpiece experiences gradient stress and heat along the depth from the grinding surface to the core.

Therefore, LAG is anticipated to be effective in fabricating gradient structures that not only achieve an optimal balance of strength and ductility but also improve machining surface quality, offering promising application prospects.
This innovative approach resulted in an excellent combination of strength and ductility, as well as enhanced machining surface quality.
Our study offers new insights into the development of LAG technology and its application in designing fcc HEAs with outstanding comprehensive mechanical properties.

Alloy 625 is a solid-solution strengthened face-centered cubic (fcc) NiCr—Mo alloy; however, precipitation hardening also plays a significant role in hardness, tensile and creep strength [6,7].

Due to its excellent wear resistance and fatigue strength, hardened AISI 52100 steel has been widely used as bulk material of critical machine elements such as high-performance bearings [1].
However, the high hardness and strength of the hardened steel bring significant challenges in precise machining.
For example, a grinding process on hardened steel typically involves substantial friction and extrusion.
Hardware affects surface properties in multiple aspects.

Hosseini and Klement [13] argued that the white layer in a machined surface was formed by two primary mechanisms: (1) the phase transformation in microstructure induced by intense heating and cooling (i. $\mathrm { e } _ { \cdot , }$ thermal effect) and (2) the refinement of grains due to severe plastic deformation (i.e., mechanical effect).

In the cutting process, the temperature on the machined surface was over the austenitization temperature of steel, and the white layer underwent a phase transformation from martensite (i.e., body-centered cubic (BCC)) to austenite (i.e., face-centered cubic (FCC)) [14].
Other scholars reported that the white layer was mainly formed by the mechanical effect.
When the temperature on a machined surface was below the temperature for a phase transformation, severe plastic deformation refined grains and formed a white layer [16].

However, limited studies have systematically addressed (1) the role of carbon atoms in forming the white and dark layers and (2) the relationship between carbide evolution and physicomechanical properties of white and dark layers.
The surface grinding experiments were conducted on hardened AISI 52100 steel; the grinding force and temperature were monitored online.
The workpiece material was standard AISI 52100 steel with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 12 mm (length × width × height).
A resin-bonded CBN grinding wheel (CBN 160 N100B 200D-15T-32H-5X) was employed.
Fig. 1a,c depicts the detailed configuration of the experimental set-up.
After grinding, the workpiece was sectioned from its ground surface by wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM), and the cross-section was polished and etched with a 4 % Nital solution for 25 s.
A representative area with a diameter of 100 µm was designated as the X-ray analysis spot within the continuous white layer.
The thickness of the etched white layers, corresponding to the removal depth, was determined from SEM observations and confirmed using a micrometer.
The scanning area and step size were set to 15 µm × 15 µm and 50 nm, respectively.
The accelerating voltage was set to 26 kV, and the working distance and tilt were set to 8 mm and 70°, respectively.
The EBSD data were acquired using Oxford Instruments AZtechCrystal software.

Fig. 2a shows the collected grinding force signals, revealing that the grinding surface was subjected to extremely high normal forces (approximately 25 N/mm) and tangential forces (approximately 10 N/ mm).
The rapid cooling drove the ground surface to undergo a martensitic transformation.
Fig. 3 shows the microstructure and morphology characteristics on the cross-section of the machined surface.
As shown in Fig. 3a, the microstructures are composed of two different layers (i.e., a white layer and a dark layer).
The enlarged view of the white layer in Fig. 3b shows that severe plastic deformation dragged the material along the grinding direction and formed multiple metal flow lines.
At a point of interest, the angle of the tangent flow line with the vertical direction is referred to as the shear angle α.
The higher magnification view of the white layer in Fig. 3c consists of a cryptocrystalline region, a rheological region, and a distorted region sequentially from the top surface inward.
The grains in this region were significantly refined with vague boundaries, leading to the term "cryptocrystalline region".
Fig. 3d demonstrates a thin sample that was first soldered to a copper grid and then thinned to 40 nm with an ion beam.

Due to the pinning effect of the carbide particle, the dislocations were firmly confined within the areas with stress concentration and they evolved into dislocation lockings (DLs).

When the martensite lattice contained supersaturated solid-dissolved carbon atoms, these carbon atoms were generally located at the midpoints of the edges and the face centers of the body-centered cubic unit cell.
Meanwhile, the distortion energy of the material affected a martensitic transformation process significantly since a martensitic transformation follows the path to minimize energy consumption.
When the distortion energy was high (i.e., more carbon atoms were solidly dissolved in the lattice), the martensite formed by phase transformation proceeded in a twinning-like manner [36].

The non-uniform stress-strain field formed around the soliddissolved carbon atoms in the α-Fe lattice strongly interacted with the substructures generated during the martensitic transformation process.

Crystalline anisotropy and the spirit of the crystal plasticity finite-element method
The elasticplastic deformation of crystalline aggregates depends on the direction of loading, i.e. crystals are mechanically anisotropic.

This phenomenon is due to the anisotropy of the elastic tensor and to the orientation dependence of the activation of the crystallographic deformation mechanisms (dislocations, twins, martensitic transformations).

A consequence of crystalline anisotropy is that the associated mechanical phenomena such as shape change, crystallographic texture, strength, strain hardening, deformation-induced surface roughening and damage are also orientation dependent.
This is not a trivial statement as it implies that mechanical parameters of crystalline matter are tensor quantities.

The statement above means that such flow curves represent an incomplete description of plastic deformation as they reduce a six-dimensional yield surface and its change upon loading to a one-dimensional (scalar) yield curve (see Fig. 1).

Another consequence of this statement is that the crystallographic texture (orientation distribution) and its evolution during forming is a quantity that is inherently connected with plasticity theory.

Texture can hence be used to describe the integral anisotropy of polycrystals in terms of the individual tensorial behavior of each grain and the orientation-dependent boundary conditions among the crystals.

Formally, the connection between shear and texture evolution becomes clear from the fact that any deformation gradient can be expressed as the combination of its skew-symmetric portion, which represents a pure rotation leading to texture changes if not matched by the rotation implied by plastic shear, and a symmetric tensor that is a measure of pure stretching.
Plastic shear hence creates both shape and orientation changes, except for certain highly symmetric shears.

Therefore, a theory of the mechanical properties of crystals must include, first, the crystallographic and anisotropic nature of those mechanisms that create shear, and second, the orientation(s) of the crystal(s) studied relative to the applied boundary conditions (e.g. loading axis, rolling plane).

Early approaches to describe anisotropic plasticity under simple boundary conditions have considered these aspects, such as, for instance, the Sachs [3], Taylor [4], BishopHill [5,6] or Kröner [7] formulations.

However, these approaches were neither designed for considering explicitly the mechanical interactions among the crystals in a polycrystal nor for responding to complex internal or external boundary conditions (Fig. 2).
Instead, they are built on certain simplifying assumptions of strain or stress homogeneity to cope with the intricate interactions within a polycrystal.
For that reason variational methods in the form of finite-element (FE) approximations have gained enormous momentum in this field.

These methods, which are referred to as crystal plasticity finite-element (CPFE) models, are based on the variational solution of the equilibrium of the forces and the compatibility of the displacements using a weak form of the principle of virtual work in a given finite-volume element.
The essential step which renders the deformation kinematics of this approach a crystal plasticity formulation is the fact that the velocity gradient is written in dyadic form.

This reflects the tensorial crystallographic nature of the underlying defects that lead to shear and consequently, to both shape changes (symmetric part) and lattice rotations (skew-symmetric part)—see Section 3.

This means that the CPFE method has evolved as an attempt to employ some of the extensive knowledge gained from experimental and theoretical studies of single-crystal deformation and dislocations to inform the further development of continuum field theories of deformation.

The general framework supplied by variational crystal plasticity formulations provides an attractive vehicle for developing a comprehensive theory of plasticity that incorporates existing knowledge of the physics of deformation processes [810] into the computational tools of continuum mechanics [11,12] with the aim of developing advanced and physically based design methods for engineering applications [13].
One main advantage of CPFE models lies in their ability to solve crystal mechanical problems under complicated internal and/or external boundary conditions.

This aspect is not a mere computational advantage but is an inherent part of the physics of crystal mechanics since it enables one to tackle those boundary conditions that are imposed by inter- and intra-grain micromechanical interactions (see Fig. 3) [14].
However, the success of CPFE methods is not only built on their efficiency in dealing with complicated boundary conditions.
They also offer great flexibility with respect to including various constitutive formulations for plastic flow and hardening at the elementary shear system level.

The constitutive flow laws that were suggested during the last decades have gradually developed from empirical viscoplastic formulations [16,17] into physics-based multiscale internal-variable models of plasticity, including a variety of size-dependent effects and interface mechanisms [9,18 26].

In this context it should be emphasized that the FE method itself is not the actual model but the variational solver for the underlying constitutive equations that map the anisotropy of elasticplastic shears associated with the various types of lattice defects (e.g. dislocations, twins, martensite).

Since its first introduction by Peirce et al. in 1982 [27] the CPFE method has matured into a whole family of constitutive and numerical formulations that has been applied to a broad variety of crystal mechanical problems (Table 1).

A conceptual advantage of the CPFE approach is that it may not only include dislocations but also other mechanisms which follow dyadic kinematics such as martensite formation [74,80], shear band formation (e.g. in glassy matter) [208,209], mechanical twinning [164166,169]and even superplastic grain boundary shear [41,45].
The CPFE method allows the user to implement these shear mechanisms including their interactions.
But it also adds complexity to the model: the use of different competing crystallographic deformation mechanisms within a CPFE model requires the formulation of local homogenization rules [1,142].

This means that at some material points only one type of deformation mechanism (e.g. dislocation slip) may occur, while in others a mix (e.g. dislocations and twins) must be considered within the same volume portion.

The latter situation requires appropriate submodels that describe the evolving fractions (e.g. of the twinned volume) and the interactions of coexisting and competing deformation mechanisms at the same field point (Fig. 4).

An aspect that increases complexity in such cases is the possibility that deformation martensite or twins may, after their formation, undergo further plastic deformation or create accommodation strains related to volume changes.
Some of these aspects will be discussed in Sections 5 and 6.
Another strength of the CPFE method is the close connection between shape change, rotation and geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) [210213].
This allows one to implement constitutive laws that treat mechanical size effects in conjunction with local orientation gradients [24].
Such lattice rotations are nowadays accessible to precise and high-resolution measurements in 2-D and 3-D so that corresponding models can be tested [95,98,171,177,214216].

Examples for small-scale applications are inter- and intra-grain mechanics, damage initiation, mechanics at interfaces, simulation of micromechanical experiments (e.g. indentation, pillar compression, beam bending), or the prediction of local lattice curvatures and mechanical size effects (see Table 1).

In such cases the experimental results may sometimes be hard to interpret without corresponding CPFE simulations that allow an experimentalist to simulate the effects of details in the contact and boundary conditions.

Many products nowadays have dimensions in the range of the grain scale, e.g. microelectromechanical systems (MEMS), bonding wires and pillars, stents, and practically all materials in electronic components.
Design of such parts increasingly requires consideration of grain-scale crystalline anisotropy.
Some applications along these lines are discussed in Section 9.
Macroscopic applications of the CPFE method occur particularly in the fields of large-scale forming and texture simulations.

These problems usually require appropriate homogenization schemes within a CPFE model since a larger number of crystals and/or phases must be considered in each representative volume element mapped at a FE integration point.

Primary engineering objectives of CPFE applications in macroscopic forming simulations are the prediction of the precise material shape after forming, thickness distribution, material failure, optimization of material flow, elastic spring-back, forming limits, texture evolution and the mechanical properties of the formed part [13,137139,145,217].
A further advantage of CPFE predictions is that they can be compared to experiments in a very detailed fashion probing a variety of quantities (Table 2).

Corresponding studies compared shape changes, forces, strains, strain paths, rate effects, texture evolution, interface response, local stresses and size effects one-to-one at different scales (Table 2).
Beyond these metallurgical and mechanical considerations numerical aspects also deserve attention.
The use of standard solvers also helps to make CPFE methods accessible to a broader community.
Since details of the FE method, the mesh and the integration procedures also play a significant role in CPFE simulations, some of these aspects are discussed in Section 8.

In summary, this review intends to demonstrate that for micro- and macro-scale mechanical problems containing dyadic degrees of freedom for shear, the CPFE method is an effective modeling platform as it can deal with the delicate interplay of different effects such as complicated boundary conditions (e.g. imposed by the surrounding microstructure or by external fields), various deformation mechanisms and their interactions (e.g. dislocation mechanics at interfaces or twins and martensite), interface properties (e.g. structural superplasticity or the HallPetch effect) and details of slip localization (e.g. shear band formation) at reasonable computational costs and by using open source or commercial solvers.
The first FE simulation was performed by Courant in 1943 [218].
The breakthrough of the method came with the publication of "The Finite Element Method in Structural and Continuum Mechanics" by O.C.

Even though it has been known since 1934 [221224] that crystalline materials deform plastically by the slip of dislocations on discrete slip systems, for a long time continuum mechanical FE simulations used isotropic material models.
The first CPFE simulations were performed by Peirce et al. in 1982 [27].
Due to computational restrictions they used a simplified set-up of two symmetric slip systems in order to study the tensile behavior of a single crystal.
These simulations were later extended to a polycrystalline arrangement by Harren et al. [225,226] using a 2-D setup with two or three slip systems.
In 1991 Becker was the first to perform simulations on the basis of the 12 slip systems of a face-centered cubic (fcc) crystal.
Using a 3-D model for the crystallographic degrees of freedom, he simulated channeldie deformation of a columnar polycrystal aggregate [106] and of a single crystal [107].
On the macroscopic side, homogenization schemes were developed for the application of the CPFE method to large-scale forming operations.

This can be achieved in different ways using, for example, texture components [138,142] or direct sampling of single orientations from the orientation distribution function (ODF) [184,227,228] (Sections 9.3 and 6.2).
All CPFE models mentioned so far used phenomenological constitutive equations (see Section 4.2) and considered dislocation slip as the only deformation mechanism.
When applying the CPFE method in new areas such as smallscale deformation or interface mechanics existing phenomenological constitutive laws are often insufficient.

Also, new classes of materials such as twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) steels or shape memory alloys show additional deformation and hardening mechanisms, i.e. twinning and/or deformation-induced phase transformations.

This most recent class of constitutive models also allows one to incorporate additional metallurgical mechanisms such as grain boundary mechanics [25,233] (Section 4.3.3) or damage initiation [199] into the constitutive description.

Concerning additional deformation mechanisms such as those that occur in TWIP or TRIP steels, extended CPFE formulations have been suggested by Kalidindi et al. [114,164], Salem et al. [169], Staroselskya and Anand [167] and Suiker and Turteltaub [234] (also see Section 5).
This section presents a detailed discussion of the different distortion measures that form the geometrical backbone of the CPFE framework.
The review is given in terms of finite deformation measures as the small distortion case can always be derived from it.

The kinematics of isothermal finite deformation describes the process where a body originally in a reference state (or "configuration"), $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ , is deformed to the current state, $\mathcal { S } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 3 } .$ , by a combination of externally applied forces and displacements over a period of time, ∆t.
In this treatment we choose the perfect single crystal as reference state.
Other possible choices of a reference state would be the state just before deformation, or in an incremental formulation, the state at any time t.
The latter has the disadvantage of a constantly changing reference state while the former might contain an undefined amount of crystal defects.
In crystal plasticity one has to distinguish three coordinate systems.
The shape coordinate system is a curvilinear system, based on the physical shape of the body, which deforms congruently with the total changes in shape occurring during deformation.

In contrast, the lattice coordinate system has coordinate axes fixed locally parallel to the crystallographic directions, i.e. the nodes of the coordinate network maintain a one-to-one correspondence with crystal lattice points during deformation except where singularities in the atomic array occur due to the defect cores.
Therefore, the space defined by the deformed lattice coordinate system is connected to ordinary Euclidean space by functions that depend on the defect content and distribution [235].
The distinction between shape and lattice distortion is critical when internal stresses are to be calculated [236].

Since these stresses arise from internal reaction forces generated when atoms experience a relative displacement from their equilibrium positions, they can only be related to lattice deformations because shape deformations do not necessarily follow the deformation of the underlying crystal lattice.

Deformations in the two types of coordinates are coincident only when no motion of crystal defects occurs, which is the usual assumption made for calculating elastic stresses from measurements of the small deformations of a coordinate system deposited on the surface or embedded within a body.

Finally, it is often convenient to describe the deformations of the overall shape of a body and its associated lattice in terms of a third reference system, laboratory coordinates, that does not deform with the body.
Computations of the deformation of both shape and lattice coordinate systems can be made in terms of their components in laboratory coordinates.
This has the practical advantage of providing a reference system that is fixed throughout the deformation of the body.
To cast this in a formal way we represent the positions of neighboring material points relative to an arbitrary origin in the reference configuration by the vector dx.
As a result of deformation, this vector is mapped into its image in the current configuration, dy = dx + du, where du is the differential total displacement vector.
These vectors are related by the total, or shape, deformation gradient, F:

The second rank tensor formed from the partial derivatives of u with respect to x is known as the shape (also total) distortion tensor, β and is a perfect differential if the deformations that produce it do not introduce any discontinuities, i.e. gaps or cleavages, in the global body.

The shape deformation can be decomposed into two components [7,211,213,237,238] (see also Fig. 5):

The "elastic" deformation, $\mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { e } } ,$ is the deformation component due to the reversible response of the lattice to external loads and displacements (as well as rigid-body rotations) while the "plastic" deformation, $\mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { p } } ,$ is an irreversible permanent deformation that persists when all external forces and displacements that produce the deformation are removed.

In this sense, transformation of the reference state by $\mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { p } }$ leads to an intermediate configuration which is free from external stresses and which is generally considered to maintain a perfect lattice.
However, this state requires that none of the dislocations which produced the permanent shape change any longer reside within the material point neighborhood, but are located at its periphery.
In reality, this assumption is typically not fulfilled, such that (balanced) internal stresses remain due to the (homogeneous) presence of dislocations within the neighborhood.
In their formulation, no residual dislocations are present in the intermediate state regardless of the vanishing of the net Burgers vector.

Making this distinction, Bilby et al. [239] refer to $\mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { p } }$ as the "dislocation deformation" and $\mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { e } }$ as "lattice correspondence functions".
In this case $\mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { e } }$ also contains a component of lattice deformation due to sources of internal stress distributed throughout the body.

At the end of the process the external loads can be removed and no lattice deformation remains, $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { p } } $ In contrast, the crystal undergoes an purely elastic shape change in Fig. 7.

In this case there are no dislocations, the lattice is distorted congruently with the external shape of the body, $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { F } _ { \mathrm { e } } ,$ ,and the external cause for the deformation must be maintained in order to preserve the change in shape; removal of the external boundary conditions causes the body to revert to the reference state.
Also the thermodynamic states of the reference and current states are different because of the stored elastic energy due to the lattice deformation.

At the onset of plastic deformation of polycrystals, mobile dislocations are first created on the slip system with the largest local resolved shear stress in the grain with the most favorable orientation.
When encountering a grain boundary these mobile dislocations accumulate in front of that interface.
Such events lead to stress concentrations at the interface that add to the external stress field at this material point.

These microplastic effects, where the local arrangement of dislocations determines the local stress, cannot be treated one-to-one in a crystal plasticity continuum mechanical framework because such models map the underlying dislocation mechanics in a phenomenological statistical or even empirical form.
However, homogenization is admissible at larger plastic strains where most of the slip activation processes can be captured by long-range stresses rather than by local ones [249].

This means that the dislocation mechanics can, beyond the microplastic regime, be homogenized in the form of statistical dislocation populations, which in turn can be embedded as constitutive rate equations in a crystal plasticity theory [19,20,25].
Two approaches for including grain boundary mechanics into dislocation-based constitutive CPFE models can be found in the literature.
In the second type of models interfaces appear as perfect obstacles that do not allow dislocation penetration events [21].
The latter assumption can be implemented in FE simulations as an additional set of boundary conditions, namely as a zero shear condition perpendicular to interfaces.

The transmission probability of incoming mobile dislocations to penetrate a grain boundary can be treated in terms of an activation concept.
The main task in this model, therefore, consists in identifying the outbound slip system on the other side of the boundary, which provides the closest geometrical match to the inbound slip system.

The smallest misalignment between the active inbound and the expected outbound slip systems leads to the smallest possible energy barrier.4 For an arbitrary transmission event, it is obvious that some incoming slip system does not, as a rule, match a corresponding one on the outbound side exactly, i.e. the shear is usually not coherent on the two sides of a grain boundary.
Therefore, in order to meet the conservation of the lattice defect vector sum when crossing an interface, misfit dislocations will be created in the grain boundary.
The additional energy required to produce such an extra misfit dislocation acts as an energy barrier for the thermally activated slip transmission event.
This barrier, hence, acts as a penalty energy for such a situation.
However, it should be interpreted in a somewhat more statistical manner.
This means that it is not required to yield a strict one-to-one correlation between incoming and outgoing dislocations rather than a match in the overall shear on either side.
Moreover, it is conceivable that the transmission event only rarely takes place owing to the local stiffening effect that it introduces.

The preceding sections focused on dislocations as carriers of plastic shear.

However, materials such as austenitic steels, TRIP steels, brass, TWIP steels and shape memory alloys deform not only by dislocation slip but also by displacive deformation mechanisms (also referred to as displacive transformations).
These mechanisms are characterized by a diffusionless collective motion of clusters of atoms where each atom is shifted by only a small distance relative to its neighbors.
Such transformations create shears with kinematics similar to that of dislocations.
Two such mechanisms and their incorporation into the CPFE framework will be discussed here, namely martensite formation [74,80] and mechanical twinning [164166,169].
Mechanical twinning proceeds by a shear mechanism, which reorients the volume affected into a mirror orientation relative to the surrounding matrix.
We discuss how the CPFE approach can be modified to include these mechanisms and how the interactions among the competing shear carriers can be considered in the constitutive formulations.
In the same year, Patel and Cohen [253] observed that during transformation, martensite develops in a preferred orientation that maximizes the transformation driving force.
Wechsler et al. [254] proposed a crystallographic model for the kinematics of martensitic transformations.
This concept was refined by Ball and James [255], who further developed the modeling concept within the energy minimization landscape.

During the last decades, various constitutive models for martensitic transformations have been proposed, such as the 1D model of Olson and Cohen [256], which was extended into a 3D model by Stringfellow et al. [257].

However, the models mentioned above have some drawbacks, i.e. most of them were derived for a small-strain framework This can lead to inaccurate predictions as martensite transformations induce locally large elastic and plastic deformations, even if the effective macroscopic deformation is relatively small.
Furthermore, an isotropic elastoplastic response is often assumed.
This constraint is quite strong, especially at the single-crystal scale, where the effect of crystallographic anisotropy cannot be neglected.
The austenitic phase is described by a single-crystal elastoplastic transformation model.
The phase transformation model of Suiker and Turteltaub [78,234,263] is applied to simulate the transformation of fcc austenite into body-centered tetragonal (bct) martensite.
This model is developed within a multiscale framework and uses the results from the crystallographic theory of martensitic transformations [254,255].
The martensitic transformation model is coupled to a single-crystal plasticity model for fcc metals in order to account for plastic deformation in the austenite.
The coupling between the transformation and plasticity models is derived using a thermodynamically consistent framework.

Arbitrary permanent changes of shape of a single crystal require the operation of any five linearly independent shear systems [4].
Low-symmetry crystal structures, e.g. hexagonal crystals with large $c / a ,$ , are typical examples for this situation.

Also, cubic metals may exhibit mechanical twinning due to a relatively strong increase in the critical shear stress at low temperatures and the rate dependence of slip in the case of bcc materials and due to the low value in the stacking fault energy in the case of fcc materials [269].
A mechanical twin formally corresponds to a sheared volume for which the lattice orientation is transformed into its mirror image across a so-called twin/composition/habitus plane (Fig. 14).
A vector of the initial lattice is moved into its new position in the twin through a transformation/rotation matrix Q.

Numerous studies have aimed at identifying the influence of the boundary conditions on mechanical twinning, focussing on temperature, grain size and stacking fault energy and their respective influence on twin nucleation and growth.
Some of the results which are required for deriving corresponding micromechanical models are summarized in the following.

Bolling and Richmann [272] and Koester and Speidel [273] found a negative temperature dependence of the twinning stress in fcc crystals, while Mahajan and Williams [274] suggested for the same structure the opposite trend.

Contradictory observations have also been reported for other crystal structures, so that the current state of knowledge seems insufficient to reach a definitive conclusion, as pointed out by Venables [275].
Only a few investigations have addressed the strain rate dependence on the twinning stress [276278].
Armstrong and Worthington [279] were the first to propose a link between the increase in the twinning stress and the decrease in the grain size by means of a HallPetch-type relation.
Later experimental studies on different materials and structures [280283] supported this suggestion.
It is worth noting that the socalled twin slope, i.e. the dependence of twin activation on the grain size, is often found to be much higher than the corresponding slope for dislocation slip [279].
It is well established that twinning occurs preferentially in low stacking fault energy materials.
This leads to a wider stacking fault, which may eventually trigger a deformation twin.
Alternatively, the notion of an effective stacking fault energy was introduced in order to consider the effect of the orientation on the splitting length between partial dislocations [285,286].

The preceding list of relevant parameters affecting mechanical twinning is, of course, not complete since other factors, such as chemical composition, strain and stress state, and precipitates, also influence strain-induced twinning [271].
The motivation for modeling mechanical twinning in a CPFE framework echoes practical as well as fundamental demands.
In each of these cases there is an interest in predicting the mechanical response, the microstructure evolution and the texture by using advanced CPFE models.

More sophisticated assumptions make use of the solution to the problem of an elastic ellipsoidal inclusion in an infinite elastic matrix given by Eshelby [303].

However, extension of such homogenization schemes from the linear to the non-linear case faces difficulties, most significantly because the stiffness, i.e. strain(rate)-sensitivity of stress, is typically inhomogeneous for a given phase due to its heterogeneous strain.
The stiffnesses are usually homogenized by using the average strain per phase as a reference input into the respective constitutive law.
Hill [308] originally introduced this incremental scheme together with a self-consistent approach.
Lebensohn and Tomé [309] later proposed a self-consistent integral formalism which links total stress to strain rate.
Further self-consistent schemes are, for example, due to Berveiller and Zaoui [310], who employed a secant modulus tensor, while Masson et al. [311] proposed an affine formulation.
Recent developments in the incremental tangent formalism can be found, for instance, in [312,313].
Grain-cluster models are an intermediate approach between the mean-field schemes and spatially resolved solutions of a representative volume element outlined above.
